Deventer
DAY-ven-ter
n. (the Ijssel town whose Brethren's school was the best in northern Europe, and whose press was among the earliest in the Netherlands)
Dutch Deventer, from a personal name or a Frankish settlement term; the town was a Hanseatic staple on the Ijssel.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Deventer is the town whose school taught the northern Renaissance and, by consequence, much of the Reformation. Its Latin school, run in close connection with the Brethren of the Common Life, reached eight or nine hundred boys under the rectorship of Alexander Hegius from 1483, and its curriculum put good Latin, some Greek and constant Scripture in front of sons of merchants and farmers; Erasmus was a pupil there, and so were a generation of men who later taught in the German and Dutch universities. The town also had one of the earliest presses in the Low Countries, printing from 1477, and for decades it produced schoolbooks and devotional works in quantity. In the revolt Deventer changed hands repeatedly, was betrayed to Spain by its English governor Sir William Stanley in 1587, and was retaken by Maurice in 1591, after which it was firmly Reformed; Caspar Sibelius was its minister and chronicler in the next century. The dictionary enters Deventer because the Reformation needed men who could read Greek and Hebrew and argue a text, and the schools that made such men were in place before there was a Reformation to use them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a grammar school as a school for teaching the languages; a staple as a settled market; to betray as to deliver into enemy hands treacherously; and erudition as learning acquired by study.

expand to see more

GRAMMAR SCHOOL, n. A school in which the learned languages are taught, as Latin and Greek.

STAPLE, n. A settled mart or market; the principal commodity of a place; an established town of trade.

BETRAY, v. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust.

ERUDITION, n. Learning; knowledge gained by study, or from books and instruction, particularly of the languages.

RECTOR, n. The master of a school; the head of a college or academy.

Modern Corruption

Ijssel town whose Latin school under Hegius taught Erasmus and the northern humanists, and whose press printed from 1477.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the contempt for learning that dresses itself as piety, and Deventer is the standing argument against it. The men who translated the Scriptures into every tongue of Europe, collated manuscripts, and answered Rome text by text had to be taught Greek and Hebrew first, by schoolmasters who were not themselves famous. The duty is laid on every man who would answer an objector: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15), and readiness of that kind is not spontaneous.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the early and thorough teaching of children, on the promise that “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). Deventer also produced a cautionary case the dictionary records: Erasmus, its most famous pupil, had the learning and declined the Reformation, which shows that scholarship is an instrument and not a conversion. The habit worth keeping is the Berean one, of men who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11), and a workman so trained “needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; Hebrew chanak (H2596), to train up; Greek apologia (G627), a defence, an answer.

expand to see more

Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to handle rightly; “rightly dividing the word of truth”, 2 Timothy 2:15.

Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train, to instruct, to dedicate; “Train up a child in the way he should go”, Proverbs 22:6.

Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, a reasoned answer; “to give an answer to every man that asketh you”, 1 Peter 3:15.

Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift by inquiry; “searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.

Greek dokimos (G1384) — approved on testing; “shew thyself approved unto God”, 2 Timothy 2:15.

Usage

"“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — nine hundred boys under Hegius from 1483."

"“to give an answer to every man that asketh you” (1Pe 3:15) — Greek and Hebrew taught to merchants' sons."

"“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — a press printing schoolbooks from 1477."
